concepts.title: Running as Root Inside a Container: Why It's Risky, and How to Avoid It
concepts.description: The default of running a container's process as root feels harmless because it's "just inside the container," but root inside a container is an identity the kernel enforces, and it becomes dangerous the moment any other layer of isolation (a mount, a capability, a kernel bug) has even a small gap. A non-root USER, dropped capabilities, and user namespace remapping each close a different part of that gap.
learningObjectives: Explain why root inside a container is not a harmless fiction, connecting it back to the fact that containers share the host's kernel.
Identify that a Dockerfile with no USER instruction runs its process as root (UID 0) by default, and explain the concrete risks that follow.
Write a Dockerfile that creates a dedicated non-root user and switches to it with USER before the container's main process runs.
Explain what a container breakout via a mounted volume or an escaped capability can actually do when the contained process is root, versus when it isn't.
Explain, at a high level, what Linux capabilities and user namespace remapping each add on top of a plain non-root USER.

sections.heading: Root Inside a Container Is Not a Harmless Fiction
sections.body:
It's tempting to think of "root inside the container" as a sandboxed, toy version of real root, unable to do anything that matters outside its own namespace. That's wrong, and the first concept in this subject explained why: a container is not a separate kernel with its own notion of privilege; it's a set of ordinary processes, isolated by namespaces and metered by cgroups, running on the *one* kernel the host is running. Root inside a container (when no user namespace remapping is configured, the default) is, to the kernel, UID 0: the same root the kernel enforces everywhere else, not a copy of it.

That matters because containers are never perfectly sealed: volumes bind specific host paths into a container, kernel vulnerabilities occasionally let a process escape its namespace boundary, and generous capabilities can hand a contained process more power than it needs. Each of those gaps is much worse when the process on the other side is root, because root is the identity that bypasses the filesystem permission checks that would otherwise limit an unprivileged process's damage. A non-root process that manages to read outside its intended sandbox is still limited by ordinary file permissions; a root process that manages the same thing is not limited by much of anything at all.

sections.heading: The Default You Get If You Do Nothing, and What It Costs
sections.body:
A Dockerfile with no `USER` instruction anywhere in it runs its main process as root. That's Docker's plain default, and it's why so many real-world images run as root without anyone having decided that on purpose. The easiest cost to demonstrate shows up with bind mounts: a root process inside a container that writes to a bind-mounted host directory writes those files as root on the host, because bind mounts don't remap UIDs by default. A runaway build script can leave root-owned files scattered across a developer's project directory, files that developer's unprivileged host user can no longer delete or edit without `sudo`.

```dockerfile
# Runs as root -- the default if you never add a USER instruction
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

The bind-mount annoyance is the visible symptom. The real risk is what root buys an attacker in a worse scenario: if this application has an unpatched dependency with a remote code execution vulnerability, an attacker who gets code execution inside this container gets it *as root*, a more dangerous foothold than the same exploit landing on an unprivileged process, because root bypasses the filesystem and capability checks that would otherwise cap the damage.

sections.heading: The Fix: A Dedicated User, and USER Before the Process Runs
sections.body:
The standard fix is to create a dedicated, unprivileged user inside the image during the build and switch to it with `USER` before the final `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT`. Everything after that instruction, including the container's running process, executes as that user instead of root:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN addgroup --system appgroup && adduser --system --ingroup appgroup appuser \
    && chown -R appuser:appgroup /app
USER appuser
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

A few details are easy to get wrong. The `chown` has to happen *before* the `USER` switch, while the build is still root and has permission to change file ownership; after `USER appuser` it fails, because that unprivileged user can't change ownership of files it doesn't own (the files `COPY` brought in belong to root). Many official base images already ship a pre-created non-root user (`node`'s images include a `node` user; `nginx`'s include an `nginx` user), so check the base image's documentation before creating another. And test that the switch took effect: a mistake in the Dockerfile can leave a container running as root even though the file looks correct at a glance, so `docker run --rm myimage whoami` should print the expected non-root username, not `root`.

sections.heading: Beyond USER: Capabilities and User Namespace Remapping
sections.body:
Switching away from root closes the most common and consequential gap, but two mechanisms go further, even though a deep dive into either is beyond this concept. Linux **capabilities** break the all-or-nothing root privilege into dozens of individually grantable powers (binding to a low-numbered port, changing file ownership, tracing another process, and so on). Docker containers already run with a reduced default capability set, which you can narrow with `--cap-drop` at run time, or loosen deliberately with `--cap-add` for the rare container that needs one specific extra power without full root.

**User namespace remapping** (`--userns-remap` at the daemon level) is a more structural mechanism: it maps root inside a container's user namespace to an unprivileged UID on the host, so even a process that is root *inside* its container is, from the host's point of view, an unprivileged user. That shrinks the blast radius of a namespace escape, since landing in a low-privilege host identity is a much smaller win for an attacker than landing in host root. It's a heavier, host-wide configuration change with compatibility trade-offs (some workloads that expect to be root can break under it), which is why a non-root `USER` in the Dockerfile is the near-zero-cost default every image should have, while user namespace remapping is an opt-in layer for environments where the extra rigor is worth the operational cost.

examples.title: The Bind-Mount Symptom: Root-Owned Files Leaking Onto the Host
examples.code:
$ docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)/output:/app/output" myimage-running-as-root
$ ls -la output/
-rw-r--r--  1 root root  1024  result.json
$ rm output/result.json
rm: cannot remove 'output/result.json': Permission denied
examples.explanation: The container's process writes result.json as root, because the process inside is root and bind mounts apply host filesystem permissions with no UID translation by default, so the file lands on the host owned by root, not by the developer's own account. The developer can't delete or edit their own build output without sudo, only because the container happened to run as root for no functional reason. It's an everyday annoyance and a small visible symptom of the same issue that makes a real compromise worse.

examples.title: Before and After: Adding a Non-Root User
examples.code:
# BEFORE -- runs as root, the default
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

# AFTER -- dedicated user, ownership fixed while still root, then switch
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN groupadd --system appgroup && useradd --system --gid appgroup appuser \
    && chown -R appuser:appgroup /app
USER appuser
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
examples.explanation: In BEFORE, every instruction, including the final running process, executes as root, since nothing in the file says otherwise. In AFTER, `groupadd`/`useradd` and the `chown` all run before `USER appuser`, while the build is still root and has permission to create users and change ownership. Reversing that order would fail, since the unprivileged user can't change ownership of files it doesn't own. From `USER appuser` onward, including the `CMD` that becomes the container's running process, everything executes as that user instead of root.

examples.title: Verifying the Switch Took Effect
examples.code:
$ docker build -t myapp .
$ docker run --rm myapp whoami
appuser
$ docker run --rm myapp id
uid=999(appuser) gid=999(appgroup) groups=999(appgroup)
$ docker run --rm myapp touch /etc/some-protected-file
touch: cannot touch '/etc/some-protected-file': Permission denied
examples.explanation: `whoami` and `id` confirm the container's process identity is the dedicated `appuser`, not root, a quick check worth running after adding a `USER` instruction, since a mistake can leave the switch ineffective while the Dockerfile looks correct. The failed `touch` against a root-owned system path is the practical payoff: this process lacks root's permissions, so even a compromised or buggy version of the application can't write anywhere it pleases in the filesystem, which is the containment a non-root user is meant to provide.

misconceptions.description: Root inside a container is a separate, contained version of root that can't actually do anything dangerous outside the container, so it doesn't matter much whether an image runs as root or not.
misconceptions.clarification: Containers share the host's one kernel -- there is no separate, sandboxed root identity invented just for containers. Root inside a container's default (unremapped) user namespace is the same UID 0 the kernel recognizes everywhere. The namespace boundary limits what that root process can SEE and interact with under normal operation, but once any other boundary has a gap (a bind-mounted host path, an overly generous capability, a kernel vulnerability allowing a namespace escape), root's kernel-level privilege determines how much damage crosses it. A non-root process hitting the same gap is limited by ordinary permission checks that root is designed to bypass.
misconceptions.fact: Containers share the host's one kernel -- there is no separate, sandboxed root identity invented just for containers.

misconceptions.description: Adding a USER instruction to a Dockerfile is all you need to do, in any order, to get a working non-root container.
misconceptions.clarification: Order matters, especially around file ownership. RUN steps that create the dedicated user, install packages, or chown application files to that user must happen WHILE the build is still root, before the USER instruction. Placing USER too early makes later RUN or chown steps fail with permission errors, since the unprivileged user lacks the privilege; a Dockerfile that puts USER appuser near the top and then tries to apt-get install or chown files won't work.

exercises.prompt: This Dockerfile builds and runs without error. What user does the running container's main process execute as, and what does docker run --rm this-image whoami print?
exercises.code:
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
hints: Scan the entire Dockerfile for a USER instruction -- is there one anywhere in it?
What is Docker's plain default identity for a container's main process when no USER instruction is ever specified?
The absence of a security-related instruction is itself a meaningful, specific default, not an unspecified or random outcome.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The process runs as root, and docker run --rm this-image whoami would print "root" -- there is no USER instruction anywhere in this Dockerfile, and Docker's default, with no USER specified, is to run the container's main process as root (UID 0).
exercises.solutionExplanation: With no explicit USER instruction, the container's main process runs as the base image's default user, which for python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm, like most common base images with no USER baked in, is root. Nothing in this Dockerfile creates another user or switches to one, so every instruction, including the final CMD that becomes the running process, executes as root, which `docker run --rm this-image whoami` confirms by printing "root".

exercises.prompt: A developer tries to add a non-root user to this Dockerfile, but the build fails with a permission error. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
USER node
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN chown -R node:node /app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
hints: Look at exactly where the USER instruction sits relative to the chown step -- which user is actually active by the time chown runs?
chown changes file ownership -- what permission does the user attempting to run it need to have in order for that to succeed?
The fix is almost always about reordering: do everything that needs root's privilege BEFORE switching users with USER.
exercises.solutionCode:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN chown -R node:node /app
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
exercises.solutionExplanation: USER node appears near the top of the file, before the COPY and RUN steps, so the build executes as the unprivileged node user from then on. That user can't write into the root-owned /app (RUN npm ci is the first step to fail, since it can't create node_modules there), and it couldn't run RUN chown -R node:node /app either, because it can't change ownership of files it doesn't own. The fix moves USER node to the end, right before CMD, so every earlier step (copying files, installing dependencies, and the chown) runs as root with permission to change ownership; only the final CMD, the running process, executes as the node user that now owns the files.

assessments.prompt: Why does running a container's process as root specifically make a bind-mounted host directory and a potential container-escape scenario meaningfully more dangerous, rather than just "a bit sloppy"?
options: Root inside a container is purely cosmetic and has no real kernel-level meaning, so the danger is only about appearances.

Root is the specific identity that bypasses ordinary filesystem permission checks and capability restrictions -- so wherever an isolation boundary has any gap (a bind mount, an escaped capability, a kernel bug), a root process can do far more damage through that gap than an unprivileged one could.
It doesn't actually matter -- namespaces alone fully contain a root process regardless of any other configuration.
Docker specifically disables all cgroup memory limits for containers running as root, so a root process can also cause unrestricted host memory exhaustion.
assessments.explanation: Because containers share the host's single kernel, a root process inside one is UID 0 as far as the kernel is concerned, and root is the identity that skips the permission checks that would otherwise cap an unprivileged process's reach through any gap in the container's isolation. The “Root inside a container is purely cosmetic…” option is wrong: root inside a container is real kernel-recognized privilege, as the first concept in this subject established. The “Docker specifically disables all cgroup memory limits…” option invents an unrelated and false claim -- cgroup limits are independent of whether the contained process happens to run as root. The “It doesn't actually matter -- namespaces alone…” option is wrong, and is the misconception this concept argues against: namespaces limit visibility under normal operation, but don't remove the extra risk root adds once any other boundary has a gap.

assessments.prompt: A container running as root writes output files into a bind-mounted host directory. What ownership do those files end up with on the host, and why?
options: They're owned by a special "nobody" account, since Docker anonymizes all bind-mount writes for safety.

They're owned by the host user who ran docker run, because bind mounts always translate the container's UID to the calling host user's UID, so a file created by root in the container always appears to belong to an ordinary user there.
Ownership is left completely undefined and varies unpredictably between otherwise identical runs.

They're owned by root on the host, because bind mounts apply host filesystem permissions directly with no UID translation by default, and the process writing them inside the container is genuinely UID 0.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer describes the bind-mount symptom: no UID translation happens by default, so a root process inside the container writing to a bind-mounted host path produces files genuinely owned by root on the host, which the developer's own unprivileged account then can't freely delete or edit without sudo. The “They're owned by the host user who…” option invents a translation mechanism bind mounts don't perform by default. The “They're owned by a special "nobody" account…” option invents an anonymization feature Docker doesn't have. The “Ownership is left completely undefined and varies…” option is wrong -- the outcome is deterministic and directly explainable by the container process's actual UID, not random.

assessments.prompt: A Dockerfile places `USER appuser` before a later `RUN chown -R appuser:appgroup /app` instruction. What happens when this image is built?
options: The chown step fails or is effectively denied, because by that point the build is running as the unprivileged appuser, which lacks permission to change ownership of files it doesn't already own.
chown automatically runs as root regardless of the currently active USER, specifically to support this exact ordering pattern.
The build succeeds, but file ownership silently reverts back to root the moment the container actually starts.
It builds fine, since USER only affects the container's runtime process, not any RUN instructions that come after it in the build, and file ownership changes during a build always run as root.
assessments.explanation: USER changes which user every subsequent instruction in the build runs as, including RUN -- so a chown placed after USER appuser executes as appuser, which typically lacks the privilege to change ownership of files, especially ones it doesn't already own. The “It builds fine, since USER only affects…” option is wrong -- USER affects every following instruction in the Dockerfile, not only the final CMD/ENTRYPOINT. The “chown automatically runs as root regardless…” option is wrong -- there's no special-case exemption that lets chown ignore the active USER; it runs with whatever privilege the current build context has. The “The build succeeds, but file ownership silently…” option is wrong -- there's no such automatic reversion; ownership is whatever the build steps actually set it to, and here the chown likely never fully succeeded in the first place.

assessments.prompt: How does user namespace remapping (--userns-remap) reduce the risk of a container-escape scenario compared to simply switching to a non-root USER inside the container?
options: It replaces namespaces entirely with a hardware-virtualized boundary functionally equivalent to a full separate VM kernel.
It automatically drops every Linux capability from every container, with no configuration required and no exceptions possible.
It maps root inside a container's own user namespace to an unprivileged, ordinary UID on the host.
It disables cgroups entirely, so a compromised process can no longer consume unbounded host resources.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer describes what user namespace remapping actually does: it's a mapping between the container's own root UID and an unprivileged host UID, so a namespace escape lands the attacker in a low-privilege host identity rather than genuine host root, shrinking the blast radius. The “It disables cgroups entirely, so a compromised…” option is wrong -- it's unrelated to cgroups, which continue to function independently. The “It replaces namespaces entirely with a hardware-virtualized…” option is wrong -- it's a UID-mapping feature within the existing namespace/cgroup model, not a hypervisor-based redesign. The “It automatically drops every Linux capability…” option is wrong -- capability dropping is a separate, related-but-distinct mechanism (--cap-drop), not something userns-remap performs, and Docker's default capability set already isn't 'everything' even without remapping.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: "It's just a container, root inside it can't actually hurt anything outside -- why bother adding a non-root USER?" Give a full answer explaining the real risk and the fix.
assessments.modelAnswer: The claim treats a container as a sealed box where root's privilege stops mattering at the container boundary, but containers share the host's one kernel, with isolation provided by namespaces and cgroups rather than a separate kernel or privilege system. Root inside a container's default, unremapped user namespace is the same UID 0 the kernel recognizes everywhere else on that host. Under normal operation the namespace boundary limits what that root process can see and touch, which is why it feels harmless day to day. But containers are never perfectly sealed: a bind-mounted host directory applies host filesystem permissions directly, with no UID translation by default, so a root process in the container writes those files as root on the host, which an unprivileged developer's account then can't modify. More seriously, if a kernel vulnerability, a misconfigured mount, or a generous capability ever lets a process cross its namespace boundary, or an attacker gets remote code execution through an unrelated application vulnerability, the damage they can do on the other side is determined by the privilege the process already had, and root is the identity built to bypass the filesystem and capability checks that would otherwise contain it. An unprivileged process hitting the same gap is still constrained by ordinary permissions. The fix costs little: create a dedicated, unprivileged user during the image build, make sure ownership changes and installs happen while the build is still root, and add a USER instruction before the final CMD so the running process executes as that user. It doesn't remove every risk (capabilities and user namespace remapping go further), but it closes the most consequential and cheapest-to-fix gap with almost no added complexity.

assessments.prompt: A security review flags that all of your containers run as root. A teammate argues it does not matter because 'it is inside a container'. How do you respond, and what changes would you make?
assessments.modelAnswer: Containers share the host kernel, so root inside a container is the same UID 0 as root on the host, restricted only by namespaces, capabilities and seccomp. If an attacker exploits the app and then a kernel or runtime bug, or a misconfiguration such as a mounted Docker socket or host path, root makes escaping to the host much easier, and even without escape they can modify anything in the container's filesystem. Fix it by creating an unprivileged user in the Dockerfile and switching with USER, making sure files the app writes are owned by that user and that it listens on a port above 1024. At runtime drop all capabilities except those needed, use a read-only root filesystem where possible, and in Kubernetes set runAsNonRoot and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false so the rule is enforced rather than remembered.

concepts.title: Minimal Base Images: Alpine, Distroless, and Why Smaller Reduces Attack Surface
concepts.description: Every package installed inside an image, whether your application calls it or not, is one more thing that can carry a vulnerability, be probed by an attacker who's gained a foothold, or need patching. A minimal base image like Alpine or a distroless image isn't just about disk space; it's about there being less inside the image for anything to go wrong with.
learningObjectives: Explain what "attack surface" means in the context of a container image and why it scales with the number of installed packages, not just image size in megabytes.
Compare a full OS base image, an Alpine-based image, and a distroless image in terms of what's actually present inside each.
Explain the specific trade-off distroless images make: no shell, no package manager, no debugging tools, in exchange for a dramatically smaller and more auditable image.
Explain why Alpine's use of musl libc instead of glibc can occasionally cause real compatibility issues, and when that risk outweighs Alpine's size benefit.
Choose an appropriately minimal base image for a given scenario, and justify the choice against its trade-offs rather than picking the smallest option automatically.

sections.heading: Attack Surface: Counting What Could Go Wrong, Not Just Megabytes
sections.body:
"Attack surface" names an intuitive idea: every package, binary, and library present in a running system is one more thing that could contain a vulnerability, one more tool an attacker who's gained a foothold could use to escalate or move laterally, and one more thing a vulnerability scanner flags and someone has to triage, patch, or accept as a risk. A full `ubuntu:22.04`-based image typically carries a package manager, a shell, core utilities, and often dozens of packages installed as transitive dependencies of what you asked for. Your application never calls into most of them, but every one is present, executable, and a potential target.

This is a different axis from raw image size, though the two often move together. A 200MB image with a rarely used compiler toolchain baked in and a 200MB image made up of application data can be the same size with very different attack surfaces; a minimal base image shrinks the *count of things present that could go wrong*, not just a number in a `docker images` listing. An attacker who gets code execution inside a container via an application-level vulnerability immediately looks for what else is available: a shell for an interactive foothold, a package manager to pull in more tools, `curl` or `wget` to exfiltrate data or fetch a second-stage payload. A minimal image doesn't prevent the original vulnerability, but none of those follow-on tools are sitting there waiting.

sections.heading: Alpine: A Smaller Linux Distribution, With One Catch
sections.body:
Alpine Linux is a complete Linux distribution, not a stripped-down Ubuntu, built from the ground up around being small, using `musl libc` instead of the far more common `glibc`, and `apk` as its package manager instead of `apt`. `alpine:3.19` itself is around 7MB, and `python:3.11-alpine` or `node:20-alpine` variants of common language images are routinely a fraction of the size of their `-slim` or full Debian-based counterparts, because the base OS underneath is smaller.

```dockerfile
FROM node:20.11.1-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

The catch is real: `musl libc` is not `glibc`, and the two aren't drop-in compatible at the binary level. Most pure-source application code never notices. But native extensions and precompiled binaries (a Python package with a compiled C extension, a Node native addon, any dependency that ships a prebuilt `glibc`-linked binary rather than compiling against whatever libc is present) can fail to load, or behave subtly differently, on Alpine because they were built assuming `glibc`. It's a recurring source of "works on the Debian-based image, breaks on the Alpine one" bugs, and it's the trade-off Alpine asks you to accept for its size: smaller, at the cost of occasionally hitting a libc-compatibility problem a `glibc`-based `-slim` image never would.

sections.heading: Distroless: No Shell, No Package Manager, No curl, On Purpose
sections.body:
Google's "distroless" images push the same idea further: rather than a smaller general-purpose Linux distribution, a distroless image contains *only* a language runtime and its minimal required system libraries: no shell (`/bin/sh` doesn't exist), no package manager, and none of the everyday tools (`curl`, `ps`, and so on) that a full image would include. It's a different design point, not just "even smaller Alpine":

```dockerfile
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app /app
CMD ["server.js"]
```

The security payoff is direct: an attacker who achieves code execution inside a distroless container has no shell to drop into, no package manager to pull in more tools, and no common utilities to abuse for reconnaissance or exfiltration. The container doesn't contain them, rather than merely not having them installed by default. The cost is the flip side: you can't `docker exec` into a running distroless container and poke around with a shell when something misbehaves in production, a common and useful debugging technique distroless gives up. That's why multi-stage builds, covered in the previous module, pair so naturally with distroless: you do the building, installing, and any exploratory shell work in a full-featured builder stage, and only the final artifact lands in the shell-less final stage that ships.

sections.heading: Choosing a Base Image Is a Trade-off, Not a Race to the Smallest Option
sections.body:
Once the size and attack-surface argument lands, it's tempting to make "always pick the smallest possible base image" a universal rule, but that overshoots the point. Alpine's musl-compatibility risk is real engineering cost: a team that hits a native-dependency incompatibility, spends a day on a cryptic failure, and pins to a `-slim` glibc-based image has made an informed trade-off in the other direction, correctly, for their dependencies. Distroless's lack of a shell is a real loss of a useful debugging tool that some teams reasonably decide isn't worth it for every service, particularly ones still under active, unstable development where the ability to `exec` in and look around earns its keep.

The durable principle isn't "smallest wins"; it's "don't ship things you don't need, and be deliberate about the ones you keep." A full Debian-based image with a shell, a package manager, and `curl` kept because your service needs to shell out to another binary at runtime is a considered choice. A full image kept out of inertia, with a debugging shell nobody has used in eight months sitting there as attack surface nobody thought about, is the anti-pattern this concept argues against. The fix is asking the question at all, and landing on Alpine, distroless, a `-slim` variant, or a full image deliberately rather than by default.

examples.title: Comparing Real Image Sizes: Full, Slim, Alpine, Distroless
examples.code:
$ docker images --format "table {{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}"
node:20.11.1              1.1GB
node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim  242MB
node:20.11.1-alpine        133MB
gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12   152MB

$ docker run --rm node:20.11.1-alpine which curl bash
# (no output -- neither exists in this image)
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/sh gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
docker: Error response from daemon: ... OCI runtime create failed: ... exec: "/bin/sh": stat /bin/sh: no such file or directory
examples.explanation: The sizes (approximate, and they vary by release) show Alpine and distroless are far smaller than the full node:20.11.1 image, but the more important detail is the second and third commands. The Alpine image has no curl or bash, so an attacker with code execution can't reach for them, not because a runtime policy blocks them but because the binaries don't exist. (Alpine isn't tool-free: busybox still provides a minimal shell plus wget and nc applets.) The distroless image goes a step further and has no shell at all, so there's no /bin/sh even for someone with legitimate access trying to debug it, the deliberate trade-off distroless makes. The `--entrypoint` flag is needed because distroless's Node image already sets node as its entrypoint.

examples.title: The musl vs glibc Trap: A Native Dependency Breaking on Alpine
examples.code:
$ docker build -t myapp:alpine -f Dockerfile.alpine .
$ docker run --rm myapp:alpine node -e "require('some-native-package')"
Error: Error loading shared library ld-linux-x86-64.so.2: No such file or directory
(needed by /app/node_modules/some-native-package/build/Release/binding.node)

# Same package, Debian-based slim image:
$ docker build -t myapp:slim -f Dockerfile.slim .
$ docker run --rm myapp:slim node -e "require('some-native-package')"
# loads and runs fine
examples.explanation: `some-native-package` ships a precompiled native binary (`binding.node`) built against `glibc`'s dynamic linker, `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, which doesn't exist on Alpine, since Alpine uses `musl libc`'s own, differently named linker. The same `package.json` and dependency version fail on Alpine and work on a Debian-based `-slim` image, purely because of the libc mismatch, with nothing wrong in the application's code. This is the trade-off described earlier: Alpine's smaller size is real, but it isn't strictly better for every dependency tree. A project whose native dependencies only ship glibc-linked prebuilt binaries may need musl-compatible alternatives, a compile from source inside the Alpine image, or the larger glibc-based -slim image.

examples.title: Multi-Stage Build Into a Distroless Final Image
examples.code:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["dist/server.js"]
examples.explanation: The build stage is an ordinary, full-featured Debian-based Node image with npm, a shell, and everything needed to install dependencies and run a build; nothing is given up during the build, since the builder stage is discarded afterward, as in the previous module's multi-stage concept. It installs all dependencies (the build step needs the dev tooling) and then runs `npm prune --omit=dev` so only production dependencies remain. The final distroless stage receives only what it needs to run, the production node_modules and the compiled dist output, and contains no shell, package manager, build tooling, or leftover source files. Someone who compromises this container through an application bug inherits none of the builder stage's tooling, because none of it crossed the stage boundary.

misconceptions.description: The main benefit of a minimal base image like Alpine or distroless is saving disk space and speeding up image pulls -- the security angle is a secondary, nice-to-have benefit.
misconceptions.clarification: Disk space and pull speed are real, visible benefits, but the security angle (attack surface) isn't secondary, and the two don't measure the same thing. A smaller image has fewer installed packages, binaries, and libraries, each one less thing that could carry a vulnerability, be used by an attacker who's gained a foothold (a shell, a package manager to pull in more tools, curl to exfiltrate data), or need to be tracked and patched. Two images could be similar in size with very different attack surfaces; size and attack surface are correlated in practice, but the security reasoning is about what's present and executable, not megabytes on disk.

misconceptions.description: Alpine-based images are a strictly better default choice than glibc-based (Debian/Ubuntu-based, including -slim variants) images, since they're smaller with no meaningful downside.
misconceptions.clarification: Alpine uses musl libc instead of the far more common glibc, and the two are not fully binary-compatible -- precompiled native dependencies (compiled C extensions, native Node addons, any package shipping a prebuilt glibc-linked binary rather than building from source against the actual libc present) can fail to load or behave differently on Alpine specifically because of this mismatch, even when the exact same dependency version works perfectly on a glibc-based image. It's a recurring, sometimes hard-to-diagnose source of "works on one base image, breaks on another" bugs. Alpine is a good default for projects without problematic native dependencies, but it's a trade-off, not a strictly dominant choice, and a team that hits this incompatibility and switches to a -slim glibc-based image is making a legitimate, informed decision, not a mistake.

exercises.prompt: An attacker exploits an unpatched dependency in a Node app and gets arbitrary code execution inside the running container. Compare what they can immediately do next if the image is node:20.11.1 (the full image) versus gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12, assuming the application itself runs identically either way.
exercises.code:
# Full image
$ docker run --rm node:20.11.1 sh -c "which curl wget nc bash apt-get"

# Distroless image
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint sh gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 -c "which curl wget nc bash apt-get"
hints: The application-level vulnerability and the resulting code execution are identical in both cases -- the question is about what's available to the attacker AFTER that point.
Recall specifically what distroless deliberately omits: not just a smaller version of the same tools, but many of them entirely absent, including any shell at all.
Consider what "code execution" even means inside a container with no shell present to run further shell commands with in the first place.
exercises.expectedAnswer: On the full node:20.11.1 image, curl, wget, bash, and apt-get are present (nc may or may not be), giving the attacker an interactive shell, tools to exfiltrate data or fetch additional payloads, and a package manager to pull in even more tools. On the distroless image, none of these exist at all -- there isn't even a shell to run further commands with, which drastically limits what the attacker can do beyond whatever the initial exploit itself directly achieved within the Node process.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The full node:20.11.1 image is a complete Debian-based system with a shell and common utilities installed, all available to anyone who gets code execution inside it: an attacker can open an interactive shell, use curl or wget to exfiltrate data or download a second-stage payload, and use apt-get to install more tools. The distroless image was built not to include any of that: no shell exists to "drop into" if the exploit tries to spawn one, and curl, wget, nc, and apt-get aren't there either (the command above fails because there's no sh to run it, which is the point). The vulnerability and the initial code execution inside the Node process are identical in both scenarios; what differs is the attacker's ability to pivot beyond that one compromised process, the attack-surface reduction a minimal or distroless image provides.

exercises.prompt: A team switches their Dockerfile's base image from node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim to node:20.11.1-alpine to shrink their image size, and their build now fails when installing dependencies. Diagnose the likely cause and describe the fix, without simply reverting the base image change.
exercises.code:
FROM node:20.11.1-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# npm ci fails with something like:
# node-gyp rebuild failed
# gyp ERR! find Python
# gyp ERR! stack Error: Can't find Python executable "python3"
hints: The failure is happening during npm ci, specifically for a dependency that needs to compile a native addon from source (node-gyp) rather than using a prebuilt binary.
Alpine ships a minimal set of packages. Does it include a C/C++ build toolchain and Python by default, the way a fuller Debian-based image does via commonly pre-installed build tooling?
The fix installs the missing build prerequisites explicitly inside the Alpine image, rather than assuming they're present the way they might have been, directly or transitively, in the slim image.
exercises.solutionCode:
FROM node:20.11.1-alpine
RUN apk add --no-cache python3 make g++
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
exercises.solutionExplanation: One of the project's dependencies compiles a native addon from source using node-gyp, which needs Python and a C/C++ toolchain (make, g++) to run the compilation. Alpine's minimal base doesn't include these, the kind of thing a minimal image strips out. The fix installs the missing build prerequisites with apk add before npm ci. This differs from the musl/glibc binary-incompatibility trap covered elsewhere in this concept: here the dependency is happy to compile against whatever libc is present, it just needs the compiler and Python available, a one-line fix rather than a fundamental incompatibility. (In a production image you'd typically do this in a build stage so the toolchain doesn't ship.)

assessments.prompt: What is the most accurate description of why a distroless image reduces attack surface more than an Alpine-based image typically does?
options: Distroless images deliberately omit a shell, package manager, and common utilities entirely, so even code execution inside the container gives an attacker no further tools to pivot with, whereas Alpine, while smaller than a full distribution, still includes a shell and a package manager (apk) by default.
Distroless images use a fundamentally more secure kernel than Alpine images do.
Distroless images cannot be exploited at all, because they don't run as containers in the traditional sense.
Alpine images always run as root by default while distroless images never do, and that is the entire difference between them.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer identifies the mechanism: distroless intentionally strips out the shell, package manager, and common CLI tools that Alpine, despite being much smaller than a full distribution, still includes by default -- that absence is what limits an attacker's options after an initial compromise, not some difference in the underlying kernel or container runtime. The “Distroless images use a fundamentally more secure…” option is false -- both run on the exact same host kernel, per the very first concept in this subject; there's no separate, more secure kernel involved. The “Distroless images cannot be exploited at all…” option is false and nonsensical -- distroless images are ordinary containers and can absolutely be exploited at the application level; they just offer less to do afterward. The “Alpine images always run as root…” option is false -- USER configuration is an independent, separate concern from which base image is chosen, and neither Alpine nor distroless automatically determines it.

assessments.prompt: A native Node.js addon works fine on node:20-bookworm-slim but fails to load with a shared-library error on node:20-alpine, using the exact same package.json and dependency versions. What's the most likely cause?
options: Alpine-based images cannot run any Node.js application that uses native addons, under any circumstances.
Alpine images always disable native code execution entirely, for security reasons, regardless of the package involved.
The Alpine image is missing a required environment variable that node:20-bookworm-slim happens to set automatically.
The native addon ships a precompiled binary linked against glibc's dynamic linker, which doesn't exist on Alpine.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the musl/glibc compatibility gap: a precompiled binary built assuming glibc's dynamic linker fails outright on Alpine, whose musl libc uses a different linker path entirely, even though the surrounding application code and dependency versions are otherwise identical. The “Alpine-based images cannot run any Node.js application…” option overstates the problem -- many native addons work fine on Alpine, particularly if they compile from source against musl rather than shipping a glibc-linked prebuilt binary. The “The Alpine image is missing a required…” option invents an unrelated environment-variable explanation not supported by the actual failure mode. The “Alpine images always disable native code execution…” option is false -- Alpine has no blanket restriction against native code; the issue is specifically a libc/linker mismatch for prebuilt glibc-linked binaries.

assessments.prompt: What is the direct operational cost a team gives up by switching a production service's final image to a distroless base, compared to keeping it on an Alpine-based image?
options: Distroless images cannot be pulled from private registries, only from public ones.
The ability to docker exec into a running container and use a shell to interactively investigate a live issue, since distroless images deliberately contain no shell binary at all.
Distroless images are incompatible with multi-stage builds and must be built as a single, monolithic stage.
Distroless images require an entirely different, incompatible container runtime than Alpine-based images do.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the trade-off distroless makes: no shell, by design, means you can't exec in and look around when something misbehaves in production, a common debugging technique that Alpine (which includes a shell) still supports. The “Distroless images cannot be pulled from private…” option is false -- distroless images are ordinary OCI images and work with any registry. The “Distroless images are incompatible with multi-stage builds…” option is false -- distroless is specifically designed to be the FINAL stage of a multi-stage build, receiving artifacts from an earlier, full-featured builder stage. The “Distroless images require an entirely different, incompatible…” option is false -- distroless images run under the exact same container runtime as any other image; nothing about the runtime itself changes.

assessments.prompt: Explain why choosing a minimal base image is a trade-off rather than a strictly dominant choice, using both Alpine's musl libc issue and distroless's lack of a shell as concrete examples, and describe how you'd decide between a full image, Alpine, and distroless for a given service.
assessments.modelAnswer: A smaller base image reduces attack surface: fewer installed packages and tools means fewer things that could carry a vulnerability and fewer tools available to an attacker who achieves code execution inside the container. But the benefit isn't free, and pretending it is leads to picking the smallest option by reflex rather than weighing the trade-off for a specific service. Alpine's cost is a compatibility risk: it uses musl libc rather than the far more common glibc, and the two aren't fully binary-compatible, so precompiled native dependencies -- a compiled C extension, a native Node addon, any package shipping a prebuilt glibc-linked binary -- can fail to load or behave differently on Alpine even when the exact same dependency works fine on a glibc-based image. That's an engineering cost: time spent diagnosing a cryptic native-library failure, or compiling dependencies from source inside the image instead of using prebuilt binaries. Distroless's cost is more direct: it has no shell, so a common debugging technique, docker exec into a misbehaving production container and look around, isn't available on that image at all. Deciding between a full image, Alpine, and distroless for a given service means actually asking what that service's dependencies look like and how it's operated: a service with no problematic native dependencies, already stable and well-understood in production, is a strong candidate for distroless, trading away shell-based debugging for the smallest possible attack surface. A service under active, less predictable development, where the team still frequently needs to exec in and investigate issues live, might reasonably stay on a slim or Alpine image a while longer, accepting a larger attack surface in exchange for that operational flexibility. And a service with native dependencies that specifically require glibc and don't build cleanly from source might correctly land on a glibc-based -slim image rather than Alpine, despite Alpine being smaller, because the compatibility risk outweighs the size benefit for that particular dependency tree. None of these is wrong in the abstract; the principle is being deliberate about which tools and packages you keep and why, not defaulting to whichever image is smallest.

concepts.title: Scanning Images for Known Vulnerabilities
concepts.description: An image is a snapshot of specific package versions frozen at build time, and every one of those versions can have a publicly known vulnerability (a CVE) disclosed against it at any point after the image was built -- a vulnerability scanner reads an image's layers to identify which package versions are present and checks them against vulnerability databases, turning "we have no idea what's in this image" into an actionable, triageable list.
learningObjectives: Explain what a container image vulnerability scanner does: identify installed package versions across all layers and cross-reference them against known-vulnerability databases.

Explain why an image that was clean when built can become vulnerable later with no changes to the Dockerfile at all, purely because a new CVE was disclosed against a package version already baked into it.
Run a scan with a representative tool and interpret a report's severity levels to decide what needs fixing now versus what can be tracked and deferred.
Explain why a smaller, more minimal base image (connecting back to the previous concept) directly reduces the number of findings a scanner has to report in the first place.
Integrate an image scan into a CI pipeline as a gate, and explain the trade-off between blocking a build on any finding versus only on findings above a chosen severity threshold.

sections.heading: What a Scanner Actually Does: Inventory, Then Cross-Reference
sections.body:
A container image vulnerability scanner does two jobs, in order. First, it builds an inventory: it walks every layer of an image (the base OS's installed packages, whatever your Dockerfile's `RUN apt-get install`/`apk add` steps added, and, for most modern scanners, application-level dependency manifests such as a `package-lock.json`, a `requirements.txt`, or a compiled Go binary's embedded module list) and produces a list of which package, at which version, is present in that image. Second, it cross-references that inventory against one or more vulnerability databases (the National Vulnerability Database and various vendor- or ecosystem-specific feeds), each of which maps a known CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier) to the package names and version ranges it affects, and reports every match.

```bash
$ trivy image myapp:1.0
myapp:1.0 (debian 12.5)
=======================
Total: 14 (UNKNOWN: 0, LOW: 6, MEDIUM: 5, HIGH: 2, CRITICAL: 1)

libssl3   3.0.11-1~deb12u2   CVE-2024-XXXX   CRITICAL   fixed in 3.0.13-1~deb12u1
```

That CRITICAL finding is specific and actionable: the `libssl3` package, at the version baked into this image, has a publicly disclosed vulnerability, and a fixed version exists upstream. The scanner isn't guessing; it's a deterministic lookup of a known package version against a known list of disclosed issues, which is why it's such a cheap, high-value check: it turns "we have no idea what's inside this image, version-wise" into a concrete, prioritizable list. (The CVE number here is a placeholder, and the output is abbreviated.)

sections.heading: Why a Clean Scan Today Doesn't Stay Clean Forever
sections.body:
This trips up people who scan an image once, get a clean report, and assume the job is done: an image's contents are static once built, with the same package versions frozen in its layers indefinitely, but the *set of known vulnerabilities* against those versions is not. A CVE can be disclosed against a package version long after it was common, stable, and widely deployed; the vulnerability didn't newly appear in the software, it was newly *discovered and reported*. An image built and scanned clean in January can show three CRITICAL findings in March with the image byte-for-byte unchanged, because public knowledge about its frozen contents changed, not the image.

The practical consequence: a one-time scan at build time is useful but not a durable guarantee. The fix is scanning *repeatedly*, on a recurring schedule, against images already sitting in a registry and already deployed, not only freshly built ones. This connects to the earlier point about pinned versions: pinning a base image tag or digest buys a reproducible build, but reproducible doesn't mean permanently secure. It means those specific versions are what you're committing to keep scanning and eventually patching, as new vulnerabilities against them are disclosed over the image's deployed lifetime.

sections.heading: Reading a Report: Severity, Fixability, and What Needs Action Now
sections.body:
A real scan report on anything beyond a nearly empty distroless image routinely returns dozens of findings, and treating every one as an urgent blocker is impractical and counterproductive: it trains whoever triages the report to ignore the whole list out of volume fatigue, CRITICAL findings included. Severity ratings (commonly LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL, following the CVSS, Common Vulnerability Scoring System, standard most scanners report against) let you triage by risk rather than raw count: a CRITICAL, remotely exploitable vulnerability in a network-facing library your application uses heavily is a very different priority than a LOW-severity issue in a rarely invoked utility that needs local access and an unlikely misconfiguration to be reachable.

Whether a fix is *available yet* matters as much as severity. A finding with a fixed version already published upstream you can act on immediately, often by rebuilding against a newer base image tag or bumping one dependency. A finding with no fix yet you can only track, mitigate around (remove the vulnerable package if it isn't needed, restrict network access to reduce exploitability, add a compensating control elsewhere), or accept as a documented risk for now. A mature process settles on an explicit policy along both axes, something like "block the build on any CRITICAL or HIGH finding that has a fix available; track MEDIUM and LOW, and anything unfixed, in a backlog with an owner and a re-check date," rather than ignoring the report or treating every line item as an immediate fire.

sections.heading: Wiring Scanning Into CI, and the Threshold Trade-off
sections.body:
Scanning's value comes from making it an automatic gate rather than something a person remembers to run now and then, which almost guarantees it eventually stops happening. A typical CI pipeline builds the image, runs the scanner, and fails the pipeline if the results violate the team's policy, before the image is pushed to a registry or deployed:

```yaml
# Illustrative CI step, not a specific vendor's exact syntax
- name: Build image
  run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
- name: Scan for vulnerabilities
  run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:${{ github.sha }}
```

`--exit-code 1` is what turns a scan into a gate: without it, most scanners print a report and exit successfully, so the CI job passes whatever was found, and the safeguard becomes log output nobody reads. The severity threshold (`--severity HIGH,CRITICAL` above) is the ongoing judgment call. Set it too strict (failing on any finding, including LOW-severity ones with no available fix) and builds fail constantly for issues nobody can act on, which trains a team to reach for `--no-verify`-style workarounds or stop trusting the gate. Set it too loose (letting HIGH and CRITICAL through) and the gate stops protecting anything. Most teams land in the middle and adjust the threshold as they learn how noisy or actionable their findings are, rather than picking one setting and assuming it's permanently right.

examples.title: A Representative Trivy Scan and What Each Column Means
examples.code:
# Illustrative output: versions, counts, and severities are examples, not a real scan
$ trivy image node:18.17.1-bookworm-slim
node:18.17.1-bookworm-slim (debian 12.1)
=========================================
Total: 23 (LOW: 9, MEDIUM: 8, HIGH: 5, CRITICAL: 1)

Library   Vulnerability     Severity   Installed Version   Fixed Version
libc6     CVE-2023-4911     CRITICAL   2.36-9+deb12u1       2.36-9+deb12u3
zlib1g    CVE-2023-45853    HIGH       1:1.2.13.dfsg-1      (no fix yet)
examples.explanation: This node:18.17.1-bookworm-slim image, scanned as-is, has 23 findings in its base OS layer before a line of application code is copied in, which is why the previous concept's push toward minimal base images matters here: fewer packages in the base image means fewer rows in this table from the outset, whatever your application adds. The libc6 row shows a CRITICAL finding with a fixed version available (2.36-9+deb12u3), immediately actionable, typically by rebuilding against a newer patch-level base image tag. The zlib1g row shows a HIGH finding with no fix published, so there's nothing to upgrade to; the options are tracking it, checking whether the vulnerable code path is reachable in this application, or accepting the risk consciously and revisiting once a fix lands.

examples.title: The Same Image, Two Different Scan Dates
examples.code:
# January: image built, scanned, clean
$ docker build -t myapp:2024-01 .
$ trivy image myapp:2024-01
Total: 0 (UNKNOWN: 0, LOW: 0, MEDIUM: 0, HIGH: 0, CRITICAL: 0)

# March: the EXACT SAME image, re-scanned, no rebuild at all
$ trivy image myapp:2024-01
Total: 2 (UNKNOWN: 0, LOW: 0, MEDIUM: 0, HIGH: 1, CRITICAL: 1)
openssl   CVE-2024-YYYY   CRITICAL   3.0.11-1~deb12u2   fixed in 3.0.13-1~deb12u1
examples.explanation: myapp:2024-01 is not rebuilt, modified, or re-pulled between January and March: it's the same image, byte for byte, under the same tag both times. What changed is external to the image: a CVE affecting the OpenSSL version frozen inside it was disclosed sometime in between. That's the mechanism behind "a clean scan today doesn't stay clean forever." The fix isn't re-scanning the same static image and hoping for a better answer; it's rebuilding against an updated base image (which will have incorporated the OpenSSL fix, assuming enough time has passed upstream) and deploying that in place of the old one.

examples.title: A CI Gate That Actually Fails the Build
examples.code:
$ docker build -t myapp:ci .
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:ci
Total: 3 (HIGH: 2, CRITICAL: 1)
...
$ echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 1
# In a CI pipeline, this nonzero exit code fails the job, blocking
# this image from being pushed to the registry or deployed anywhere
examples.explanation: The `--exit-code 1` flag converts an informational scan into an enforcement gate: without it, Trivy prints the same report but exits 0, which most CI systems read as "this step succeeded," letting a build with a CRITICAL vulnerability reach deployment with nobody's attention drawn to it. `--severity HIGH,CRITICAL` narrows what can fail the build to the two highest tiers, so LOW and MEDIUM findings still appear in the report (worth tracking) without blocking every build over lower-priority issues that often have no immediate fix, the threshold trade-off discussed above.

misconceptions.description: Once an image passes a vulnerability scan with a clean report, it's permanently verified safe -- there's no need to scan it again unless the Dockerfile itself changes.
misconceptions.clarification: An image's own contents are frozen once built, but the universe of PUBLICLY KNOWN vulnerabilities against those exact package versions keeps growing over time, entirely independent of the image itself changing at all. A CVE can be disclosed against a package version that's already been sitting, unmodified, inside a deployed image for months -- the vulnerability was always technically present in that code, it simply hadn't been publicly discovered and reported yet at the time of the original clean scan. A durable practice re-scans images already sitting in a registry or already deployed on a recurring schedule, not only at the moment they're freshly built, precisely because a scan's result is a snapshot of current public knowledge at the moment it ran, not a permanent certificate.
misconceptions.fact: An image's own contents are frozen once built, but the universe of PUBLICLY KNOWN vulnerabilities against those exact package versions keeps growing over time, entirely independent of the image itself changing at all.

misconceptions.description: The right policy for a vulnerability scanner in CI is to fail the build on any finding at all, at any severity, to be maximally safe.
misconceptions.clarification: Blocking on every finding, regardless of severity or whether a fix exists, tends to backfire: a real scan of anything beyond a nearly empty image routinely turns up dozens of LOW and MEDIUM findings, many with no fix available, and failing every build over issues nobody can act on trains a team to work around the gate or stop reading the report out of noise fatigue, which defeats the point of having it. A more durable approach sets an explicit severity threshold (commonly blocking only on HIGH/CRITICAL findings that have an available fix) and routes lower-severity or currently-unfixable findings into a tracked backlog with an owner and a revisit date, rather than either extreme of ignoring the scanner or blocking on absolutely everything it reports.

exercises.prompt: A team builds and scans myapp:1.0 in January and gets a clean report (zero findings). They never rebuild it, never touch the Dockerfile, and never re-pull the base image -- but a serious CVE affecting a package version already frozen inside myapp:1.0 is disclosed publicly in April. What does re-scanning the exact same, unmodified myapp:1.0 image in April show, and why?
exercises.code:
# January
$ trivy image myapp:1.0
Total: 0

# April -- same image, no rebuild, no changes at all
$ trivy image myapp:1.0
hints: The image's own bytes haven't changed between January and April at all -- what specifically DID change in that time?
A vulnerability scanner's report reflects the state of PUBLIC KNOWLEDGE about known vulnerabilities at the moment the scan runs, not some property baked permanently into the image at build time.
The vulnerability was arguably already technically present in that package version all along -- what changed was whether anyone had disclosed it yet, not whether the underlying code was exploitable.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The April scan of the identical, unchanged myapp:1.0 image now reports the new finding, because the CVE was disclosed against a package version that was already frozen inside the image the whole time -- the vulnerability database the scanner checks against grew to include it between January and April, even though the image itself never changed at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: myapp:1.0's contents, every package at every version, have been static since it was built in January. What changed is external to the image: the public vulnerability databases scanners check against were updated with a newly disclosed CVE affecting a package version already frozen inside it. A scanner's report is a snapshot of what's known publicly, right now, about the package versions present: the January report reflected public knowledge in January, and the April report reflects April's, applied to the same package inventory both times. That's why a mature process re-scans images on a recurring schedule even when nothing about the Dockerfile or build has changed.

exercises.prompt: A team adds a vulnerability scan to their CI pipeline, and it clearly finds a CRITICAL vulnerability in its printed report -- but the CI job still shows green (passing), and the vulnerable image gets deployed anyway. Find the bug in their CI configuration.
hints: The scanner is clearly running and clearly printing a report that shows the CRITICAL finding -- so the scan itself isn't the problem.
Think about what actually makes a CI step "fail" versus just "produce output" -- what does the scan command's own process exit code have to do with that?
By default, most scanners are built to report findings without treating their own presence as an automatic failure -- something explicit usually has to opt into that behavior.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Trivy by default prints its findings but exits with code 0 (success) even when it finds vulnerabilities. Reporting and failing are separate behaviors, and without a flag saying otherwise a CI system reads exit code 0 as "this step succeeded" and continues to the deploy step whatever the report said. The fix adds --exit-code 1 (return a nonzero exit code when matching findings are present) with a severity filter like --severity HIGH,CRITICAL, so the scan step fails the CI job when a CRITICAL vulnerability like this one is found, stopping the pipeline before the deploy step and turning informational log output into an enforced gate.

assessments.prompt: An image was built and scanned clean six months ago and has not been rebuilt since. A teammate argues it's still safe today because "it passed the scan." What is the strongest response to that claim?
options: The claim is correct -- once an image passes a scan, its contents are permanently verified against every vulnerability that could ever be disclosed against those package versions.

The claim is irrelevant, because vulnerability scanners only check for vulnerabilities in the application's own source code, not in OS or dependency packages, so the scan result has nothing to do with the image's ongoing safety anyway.

The claim is incomplete -- the scan's clean result only reflected the state of public vulnerability knowledge six months ago; new CVEs can be, and routinely are, disclosed since then against the exact package versions already frozen inside that unchanged image, so it should be re-scanned on a recurring basis, not just at build time.
The claim is wrong because images automatically become insecure over time regardless of scanning, purely due to age, independent of any actual vulnerability disclosures.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer identifies that a scan's result is a snapshot of public vulnerability knowledge when it ran, not a permanent guarantee: new CVEs disclosed after that scan against package versions already frozen in the unchanged image are the gap that makes recurring re-scanning necessary. The “The claim is correct -- once…” option is the actual misconception this concept warns against -- a scan cannot verify against vulnerabilities that haven't been disclosed yet at scan time. The “The claim is irrelevant, because vulnerability scanners…” option is factually wrong -- scanners specifically focus heavily on OS packages and dependency manifests, which is the entire point of the tool. The “The claim is wrong because images automatically…” option is wrong for a different reason: age by itself isn't the mechanism; new CVE disclosures against already-present package versions create the new risk, not the mere passage of time.

assessments.prompt: What two distinct steps does a container image vulnerability scanner perform, in order?
options: It first asks the image's own maintainers to supply a manifest of known issues, then verifies that manifest's accuracy against the image's actual contents.
It first runs the application in a sandbox to observe its live runtime behavior, then flags any behavior that looks anomalous.

It first builds a precise inventory of exactly which packages, at exactly which versions, are present across all of an image's layers, then cross-references that inventory against public vulnerability databases to find matching known CVEs.
It first automatically patches every known vulnerability it can, then reports which ones it fixed.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer describes the two-step mechanical process: inventory (identify exact package/version pairs across every layer, including OS packages and application dependency manifests) followed by cross-reference (match that inventory against CVE databases like the NVD and vendor feeds). The “It first automatically patches every known vulnerability…” option is false -- scanners identify vulnerabilities; they don't automatically patch anything. The “It first asks the image's own maintainers…” option is false -- scanners work independently of any manifest a maintainer might supply; they inspect the image's actual contents directly. The “It first runs the application…” option is false -- this describes a runtime/behavioral analysis technique, not what an image vulnerability scanner (which works on static image contents) actually does.

assessments.prompt: A team configures CI to fail the build on ANY vulnerability finding at all, regardless of severity or whether a fix is even available yet. What is the most likely practical consequence?
options: Builds start failing constantly over low-severity or currently-unfixable findings nobody can immediately act on.
This configuration automatically causes the scanner itself to downgrade every finding to LOW severity so the pipeline keeps passing.
This policy has no meaningful downside at all, since more aggressive scanning is always strictly better regardless of the policy wrapped around it.
This guarantees the team's images are permanently free of every vulnerability that could ever be disclosed against them, forever.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the warning about over-strict gating: a fail-on-anything policy produces so much noise from low-severity and unfixable findings that teams start ignoring or routing around the gate, which is functionally the same as not scanning at all -- exactly why a severity threshold plus a tracked backlog for lower-priority findings is the more durable approach. The “This guarantees the team's images are permanently…” option is false -- a scan can only reflect currently known CVEs; it cannot guarantee protection against anything not yet disclosed. The “This policy has no meaningful downside…” option is false -- the concept explicitly identifies this as having a real downside (noise fatigue, workaround behavior). The “This configuration automatically causes the scanner itself…” option is false -- scanners report severities based on actual CVSS data; a CI policy has no ability to alter how the scanner itself classifies findings.

assessments.prompt: Explain what a vulnerability scanner actually does at a mechanical level, why a smaller base image (connecting to the previous concept) tends to produce a shorter, more manageable report, and how you'd set up a sane CI policy around scan results rather than either ignoring them or blocking every build on any finding.
assessments.modelAnswer: A vulnerability scanner works in two steps: it inventories an image by walking every layer and identifying which packages, at which versions, are present (base OS packages, anything your Dockerfile installed, and typically application-level dependencies read from manifests like package-lock.json or requirements.txt), then cross-references that inventory against public vulnerability databases that map known CVEs to the package versions they affect, reporting every match with a severity rating and, when one exists, a fixed version to upgrade to. A smaller base image, per the previous concept, shrinks the first half of that process: an Alpine or distroless image has far fewer packages than a full Debian or Ubuntu-based image, so the inventory has fewer rows to check. Attack surface reduction and a shorter scan report are two views of the same fact: there's less installed software to have something wrong with. A sane CI policy avoids both extremes. Ignoring the scanner's output defeats its purpose, since actionable findings would reach production unnoticed; failing the build on any finding, including low-severity issues with no fix yet, produces so much build-blocking noise that teams work around the gate or stop paying attention, which is the same as never having scanned. A workable middle ground sets a severity threshold (commonly failing only on HIGH or CRITICAL findings that already have a fix available, since those are serious and immediately actionable), keeps lower-severity or currently unfixable findings in the report for a tracked backlog with an owner and a revisit date, and re-runs the scan on a recurring schedule against deployed images, since new CVEs keep being disclosed against already-frozen package versions.
